questions.stem: Use the clinic note to fill in the diagram: the problem this client with COPD most likely has, 2 actions for the nurse, and 2 parameters to track.

actions.text: Hold theophylline and notify the provider
Place the client on a cardiac monitor
Give the next theophylline dose with food
Encourage strong coffee to relieve nausea
Increase the ciprofloxacin to clear the infection faster

parameters.text: Daily body weight on one scale

rationale.correct: Theophylline has a narrow range (about 10 to 20 mcg/mL); interacting drugs such as ciprofloxacin raise it. Hold it, monitor the heart and recheck the level.

perOption.c1: Ciprofloxacin slows theophylline clearance; nausea, tachycardia, tremor and a level of 28 fit toxicity.
perOption.p1: Tachydysrhythmias are a key toxic effect.
perOption.p2: Guides when to restart and at what dose.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

exhibits.title: Clinic note
exhibits.body: A 70-year-old client with COPD takes theophylline ER 300 mg twice daily. Ciprofloxacin was started 4 days ago for a urinary infection. Today: nausea, vomiting, tremor, HR 128/min, irregular. Theophylline level 28 mcg/mL (therapeutic 10 to 20). Glucose 96 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has been treated for 3 days. For each trend, choose how the nurse should interpret it.

cells.text: Crackles right base to dullness and absent sounds right base

options.text: New finding suggesting a pleural effusion

rationale.correct: Fever and white count are improving, but a static oxygen need with new dullness suggests a parapneumonic effusion that needs imaging.

perOption.b2:a: Oxygenation should improve by day 3; check for effusion, empyema or another cause.
perOption.b2:c: A plateau with a falling SpO2 needs review.
perOption.b3:a: Dullness with absent breath sounds suggests fluid.
perOption.b3:b: Resolution brings clearing crackles, not dullness.

questions.stem: At the start of the day shift on a pulmonary unit, four clients are assigned to the nurse. Whose bedside should the nurse go to first?

options.text: A client with COPD on 2 L/min whose SpO2 is 89% and who is eating breakfast
A client on day 2 of TB treatment in airborne isolation who is asking for a newspaper
A client with a chest tube that stopped tidaling an hour ago who is now short of breath
A client with asthma whose peak flow is 75% of personal best before the morning inhaler

rationale.correct: New dyspnea with a change in chest tube function is the most unstable situation.

perOption.a: Within the 88% to 92% target for chronic CO2 retention.
perOption.b: A stable request that can wait.
perOption.c: Loss of tidaling with new dyspnea suggests a blocked tube or a re-expanding problem; it needs assessment now.
perOption.d: In the yellow zone, needing the scheduled treatment, but stable.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of carbon monoxide poisoning and inhalation injury.

questions.stem: For each statement about the client, indicate whether it is accurate or inaccurate.

rows.text: The SpO2 of 99% shows the tissues are well oxygenated.
CO binds hemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen.
High-flow oxygen shortens the half-life of carboxyhemoglobin.
Hoarseness after smoke exposure can progress to airway obstruction within hours.
Without skin burns, inhalation injury is unlikely.

rationale.correct: CO blocks oxygen carriage while SpO2 and PaO2 stay normal; inhalation injury can swell the airway without skin burns.

perOption.r1:c1: Standard pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin.
perOption.r1:c2: Standard pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin.
perOption.r2:c1: So little CO blocks much oxygen transport.
perOption.r2:c2: So little CO blocks much oxygen transport.
perOption.r3:c1: From about 4 to 5 hours on room air to about 1 hour on 100% oxygen.
perOption.r3:c2: From about 4 to 5 hours on room air to about 1 hour on 100% oxygen.
perOption.r5:c1: Inhalation injury occurs without skin burns.
perOption.r5:c2: Inhalation injury occurs without skin burns.

questions.stem: Before discharge, the client describes home safety plans. For each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "I'll put a CO detector near the bedrooms."
"The smoke alarm will also warn me about carbon monoxide."
"I'll test the alarms every month."
"It's fine to run the generator in the garage with the door open."
"If I get headaches that improve when I leave the house, I'll get it checked."
"I'll plan two ways out of each room."

rationale.correct: Teaching covers CO detectors, generator safety, alarm testing and an escape plan.

perOption.r1:c1: CO detectors near sleeping areas give early warning.
perOption.r1:c2: CO detectors near sleeping areas give early warning.
perOption.r2:c1: Most smoke alarms do not detect CO unless they are combination units.
perOption.r2:c2: Most smoke alarms do not detect CO unless they are combination units.
perOption.r4:c1: Generators must run outside, away from windows and doors.
perOption.r4:c2: Generators must run outside, away from windows and doors.
perOption.r5:c1: A classic sign of CO exposure.
perOption.r5:c2: A classic sign of CO exposure.
perOption.r6:c1: Part of a fire escape plan.
perOption.r6:c2: Part of a fire escape plan.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of flail chest.

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: The flail segment moves inward on inspiration because {{b1}}. The client's hypoxemia is likely to {{b2}} over the next 2 days because {{b3}}.

options.text: negative pressure in the chest pulls the unsupported segment in
the client is breathing too deeply
the contused lung fills with blood and edema
the client will be more active

rationale.correct: A flail segment moves paradoxically; contusion hypoxemia worsens over 24 to 72 hours.

perOption.b1:a: The segment is detached from the rib cage.
perOption.b1:b: The movement is from the chest wall.
perOption.b2:a: Contusions evolve with swelling and bleeding into the lung.
perOption.b2:d: Pain contributes, but the contusion progresses.
perOption.b3:a: Gas exchange falls as alveoli fill.

questions.stem: For each complication, indicate how likely it is in the first 72 hours.

rows.text: Atelectasis and pneumonia from shallow breathing
Respiratory failure as the contusion evolves
Pulmonary edema made worse by large IV fluid volumes
Hemothorax or pneumothorax from rib ends
Diabetic ketoacidosis

perOption.r1:c2: Pain prevents deep breaths and coughing.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues in viral pneumonia on high-flow oxygen.

questions.stem: The ROX index helps predict whether high-flow oxygen will fail. ROX = (SpO2 / FiO2) / respiratory rate. Using the 1000 values, what is the client's ROX index? Record your answer to one decimal place.

rationale.correct: SpO2 92 / FiO2 0.60 = 153.3. 153.3 / 30 = 5.1. A ROX of 4.88 or more suggests high-flow oxygen is likely to succeed; below 3.85 suggests failure and a need to escalate.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

options.text: lower, since the ROX is above 4.88, but the client needs close watching

perOption.b1:c: The client is still severely ill.
perOption.b2:c: Needs treatment but does not indicate intubation.
perOption.b2:d: Common and not a marker of failure.

questions.educationalObjective: Take action for multiple drug-induced emergencies.

questions.stem: Before discharge, the client and partner discuss cold remedies. For each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "I'll ask the pharmacist before buying any cold or sleep medicine."
"Nighttime cold products with antihistamines are safe if I take them only at night."
"Decongestants are a problem with my prostate and my eyes."
"Cough medicine with dextromethorphan is fine with my sertraline."
"Saline nasal spray and honey are safer choices for my symptoms."
"I'll take two cold products together if one isn't strong enough."

rationale.correct: Older adults should check cold remedies with a pharmacist and avoid sedating antihistamines, decongestants and serotonergic cough medicines.

perOption.r2:c1: Sedating antihistamines are a risk for older adults at any time.
perOption.r2:c2: Sedating antihistamines are a risk for older adults at any time.
perOption.r4:c1: Together they can cause serotonin syndrome.

caseStudies.title: Carbon monoxide poisoning with smoke inhalation

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 0230
exhibits.body: A 52-year-old client was pulled from a house fire after about 15 minutes in a smoke-filled bedroom. The client has a severe headache, is confused, and vomited once. Soot is in the nose and mouth, nasal hairs are singed, and the voice is hoarse. No burns to the skin. Oxygen 2 L/min by nasal cannula was started by paramedics.

rows.label: ECG
cells: Sinus tachycardia, ST depression in V4 to V6

exhibits.title: Trauma unit, admission
exhibits.body: A 45-year-old client was the driver in a car crash. Left ribs 4 to 7 are each broken in two places. During inspiration, a section of the left chest wall moves inward while the rest of the chest expands. CT shows a left lung contusion. The client rates pain 9 of 10, breathes shallowly and will not cough.

caseStudies.title: Viral pneumonia on high-flow nasal oxygen

exhibits.title: Step-down unit, 1000
exhibits.body: A 59-year-old client with viral pneumonia from COVID-19 (day 8 of illness) has bilateral infiltrates. History: obesity, type 2 diabetes. The client is on high-flow nasal cannula at 50 L/min and FiO2 0.60. The client is anxious and talks in short sentences.

caseStudies.title: Over-the-counter cold medicines in an older adult

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 1600
exhibits.body: A 78-year-old client with benign prostatic hyperplasia, hypertension, narrow-angle glaucoma and depression (sertraline 100 mg daily) took a "nighttime multi-symptom cold" product four times in 24 hours, plus extra cough syrup. The product contains pseudoephedrine, diphenhydramine and dextromethorphan. The client's partner says the client is "seeing things" and has not urinated since morning.

rows.label: Mental status
cells: Agitated, confused, picking at the air

rows.label: Neuromuscular
cells: Tremor, inducible ankle clonus, brisk reflexes

rows.label: Eyes
cells: Severe right eye pain, blurred vision, halos, mid-dilated pupil
